items.question_text: Someone stands at the top of a sloping hill and throws a stone purely horizontally, giving it speed v₀. Using an x-y axis system with its origin at the throwing point, work out the x and y coordinates of the spot on the hillside where the stone eventually lands.
items.figure_description: The hill's top is at the origin (0,0) of an x-y axis system, with the x-axis horizontal (pointing in the direction of throw) and the y-axis vertical. The stone is thrown horizontally with speed v₀ along the positive x direction from the origin. The hillside slopes downward from the origin at angle θ below the horizontal x-axis, and the stone's curved path meets this sloped hillside at a point (x, y), with y measured as negative below the origin.

solution.approach: Write the horizontal and vertical distances travelled as functions of time, then find where the path meets the sloped hill surface.

steps.text: Use the axes given in the question: origin at the launch point, x horizontal along v₀, y vertical and positive upward. Then x(t) = v₀t and y(t) = −½gt².
The hill surface is the straight line y = −x tanθ through the origin; set the path equal to this line and solve for t.
Substitute this time back into x(t) and y(t) to get the landing coordinates.

final_answer.value: The stone lands at (x, y) = (2v₀²tanθ/g, −2v₀²tan²θ/g); the negative sign shows the landing point lies below the launch point, as in the figure.

common_mistakes.text: Writing the incline's equation the wrong way round, x = y tanθ instead of y = x tanθ, which changes the tanθ power in the landing time and coordinates.

items.question_text: Assertion: Whenever the acceleration of a particle does not change, the only path it can trace is a parabola. Reason: The trajectory in projectile motion is a parabola because, near the ground, the acceleration is treated as unchanging.

options.label: (a)
options.text: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

options.label: (b)
options.text: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

options.label: (c)
options.text: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.

options.label: (d)
options.text: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

solution.approach: Constant acceleration alone does not force a curved path; a velocity launched along the acceleration direction gives a straight line instead.

steps.text: Consider a particle given an initial velocity pointing along the same line as the constant acceleration, for example thrown straight up under gravity.
Its sideways coordinate never changes, since there is no sideways velocity and no sideways acceleration.
So this particle moves along a straight vertical line, not a parabola, even though its acceleration is constant the whole time.
This counterexample shows the Assertion is false: constant acceleration does not by itself force a parabolic path.

The Reason is a separate, true statement — projectile motion is parabolic because its acceleration is treated as constant at low heights — but the Reason being true does not make the Assertion true, so the Assertion is false and the Reason is true.
steps.why_this_step: This combination matches the option for a false Assertion with a true Reason.

final_answer.value: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Believing constant acceleration always produces a curved path, missing the case where the initial velocity points along the acceleration.
Judging both statements true without checking whether a straight-line counterexample exists under constant acceleration.

items.question_text: A trainer launches a baseball to a teammate, sending it off at 20 m/s at 45° above horizontal. The instant the throw happens, the teammate is standing 50 m away. Using g = 10 m/s², determine the running speed and direction the teammate needs so the catch happens exactly at the height the ball started from.

solution.approach: Find where the ball lands using the range formula, then find the speed needed to close the remaining gap in the time of flight.

steps.text: Find the horizontal and vertical parts of the throw's initial velocity.
Find the time of flight, since the ball returns to the height it was released at.
Find how far the ball travels horizontally in that time.
The player starts 50 m away and must reach the point 40 m away where the ball lands, so find the distance to close.
Divide this distance by the time of flight for the running speed; this gives the final answer.
steps.equation: v = 10/(2√2) = 5√2/2 ≈ 3.54 m/s, running toward the trainer

final_answer.value: about 3.54 m/s, running toward the trainer

common_mistakes.text: Dividing the full initial separation of 50 m by the time of flight, instead of the 10 m gap left to close, gives a wrong speed of about 17.68 m/s.

items.question_text:
Two particles are launched at the same instant, moving horizontally, from two different points on a riverbank that sit at some height above the water. Particle 1 has initial speed v₁ = 5 m/s and particle 2 has initial speed v₂ = 7.5 m/s. Both particles land in the water simultaneously. The first particle lands at a horizontal distance s = 10 m from the bank.
(a) Find how long each particle remains airborne before hitting the water.
(b) Find the height of the riverbank above the water surface.
(c) Work out where the second particle lands in the water, measured from the bank.

solution.approach: Both particles fall from the same height for the same time; the first particle's range gives that time, which then gives the height and the second particle's landing point.

steps.text: Find the time of flight from the first particle's horizontal speed and its landing distance.
Since both particles are in the air for the same time and start from the same height, use free fall from rest to find that height.
The second particle travels horizontally at its own constant speed for the same time to find where it lands.
State the three results together.
steps.equation: (a) t = 2 s, (b) h = 19.6 m, (c) x₂ = 15 m from the bank

final_answer.value: (a) t = 2 s, (b) h = 19.6 m, (c) second particle lands 15 m from the bank

common_mistakes.text: Taking the horizontal distance s = 10 m itself as the fall height instead of computing it from the time of flight gives 10 m, well short of the correct 19.6 m.

items.question_text: A bullet launched at 30° to the horizontal lands 3.0 km from where it was fired. If the launch angle is changed while everything else about the shot is kept the same, is it possible to strike a target sitting 5.0 km away? The bullet leaves the barrel at a constant speed, and air drag can be ignored.

solution.approach: Find the maximum possible range at this fixed muzzle speed and compare it with the target distance.

steps.text: Write the range formula and use the given range at 30° to relate it to the muzzle speed.
The maximum range for a fixed speed occurs at 45°, where sin2θ = 1, so the maximum range equals u²/g.
Compute this value.
Compare this maximum with the target distance to answer the question; this gives the final answer.
steps.equation: 5.0 km is greater than 3.46 km, so no angle can reach the target

final_answer.value: No. The maximum range at this muzzle speed is about 3.46 km, less than 5.0 km, so no angle of projection can hit the target.

common_mistakes.text: Dividing the given range by sin30° instead of sin60° gives a wrong maximum range of 6.0 km, wrongly suggesting the target can be hit.

items.question_text: A projectile launches at elevation angle α above the horizontal. Viewed from the launch point, after t seconds it appears to be at elevation angle β. Determine the launch speed of the projectile.

solution.approach: The apparent elevation angle is the angle of the position vector, so its tangent equals the ratio of the vertical to horizontal displacement.

steps.text: Write the horizontal and vertical displacements at time t for a projectile launched at angle α with speed u.
steps.equation: x = u cos α · t, y = u sin α · t − ½gt²

steps.text: The apparent elevation β is the angle the line from the launch point to the particle makes with the horizontal, so its tangent is y divided by x.
steps.equation: tan β = y/x = tan α − gt/(2u cos α)

steps.text: Solve this equation for u.
steps.equation: u = gt / [2 cos α (tan α − tan β)]

steps.text: Rewrite the denominator using the difference formula for sine to reach the standard form.
steps.equation: u = gt cos β / [4 sin(α − β)]

final_answer.value: u = gt cos β / [4 sin(α − β)]

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting the ½ in the vertical displacement formula doubles the g t term inside the tangent equation and gives twice the correct initial velocity.

items.question_text:
A lift is moving upward, accelerating at 1 m/s². At the moment its speed reaches 2 m/s, a stone is thrown from the lift's floor, its speed relative to the lift being 2 m/s, launched upward at 30° elevation.
(a) Work out how long the stone takes before it lands back on the lift's floor.
(b) Draw the trajectory the stone follows, as seen by someone standing outside the lift.
(c) Suppose instead the lift accelerates downward at a rate equal to g. Describe how the stone's motion would then differ.

solution.approach: Inside the accelerating elevator the stone feels an increased effective gravity g + a, so its relative flight time follows the usual projectile formula with that effective value.

steps.text: Find the stone's vertical velocity component relative to the elevator at launch.
Inside the upward-accelerating elevator, the effective downward acceleration felt by the stone relative to the elevator is g plus the elevator's own acceleration.
steps.equation: g_eff = g + a = 10 + 1 = 11 m/s² (taking g = 10 m/s²)

steps.text: Use the usual projectile time-of-flight formula with this effective gravity to find when the stone returns to the elevator floor.
steps.equation: t = 2v_rel/g_eff = 2×1/11 = 2/11 s ≈ 0.18 s, with g = 9.8 m/s², g_eff = 10.8 m/s² and t ≈ 0.185 s

steps.text: For an observer outside the elevator, the stone's initial velocity is the elevator's velocity plus the stone's velocity relative to the elevator. After release the stone moves under ordinary gravity g alone, so it follows a normal parabolic path while the elevator floor keeps accelerating away beneath it.
steps.equation: vₓ = 2cos30° ≈ 1.73 m/s, v_y = 2 + 2sin30° = 3 m/s, both measured from the ground

steps.text: If the elevator instead accelerates downward at g, it is in free fall, so the effective gravity felt inside it becomes zero.
State all three results together.
steps.equation: (a) t = 2/11 s ≈ 0.18 s taking g = 10 m/s² (≈ 0.185 s with g = 9.8 m/s²), (b) a parabola in the ground frame with initial velocity 1.73 m/s horizontal and 3 m/s upward, (c) with downward acceleration g the effective gravity inside is zero, so relative to the elevator the stone moves in a straight line at constant velocity and never returns to the floor

final_answer.value: (a) t = 2 sin30°·2/(g + 1) = 2/11 s ≈ 0.18 s taking g = 10 m/s² (≈ 0.185 s with g = 9.8 m/s²), (b) a parabola in the ground frame with initial velocity 1.73 m/s horizontal and 3 m/s upward, while the elevator floor accelerates away beneath the stone, (c) with downward acceleration g the elevator is in free fall, so relative to it the stone moves in a straight line at constant velocity and never returns to the floor

common_mistakes.text: Using ordinary gravity g instead of the effective gravity g + a for the time in part (a) gives 0.2 s instead of the correct 0.18 s.

items.question_text: Assertion: We describe projectile motion as two-dimensional even though the motion actually happens within three-dimensional space. Reason: Even in three-dimensional space, the motion stays confined to a single flat plane.

options.label: (a)
options.text: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

options.label: (b)
options.text: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

options.label: (c)
options.text: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.

options.label: (d)
options.text: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

solution.approach: Projectile motion happens in three-dimensional space, but the path always lies inside one fixed plane set by the launch velocity and gravity.

steps.text: Gravity always points straight down, and the initial velocity has some fixed direction in space.
These two directions together fix a single plane that contains the whole path, since nothing pushes the particle sideways out of that plane.
Because the entire trajectory stays inside this one plane, only two coordinates are needed to describe the motion at any instant.
This is exactly why projectile motion is called two dimensional even though it happens somewhere in three-dimensional space, so the Assertion is true and the Reason correctly explains it.
steps.why_this_step: The Reason states the geometric fact — motion confined to one plane — that directly gives the Assertion its two-dimensional description.

final_answer.value: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

common_mistakes.text: Thinking that because projectile motion happens in three-dimensional space, the Reason about it lying in one plane must be false.
Agreeing both statements are true but doubting that the Reason actually explains the Assertion, when it directly does.

items.question_text: Two balls, A and B, are thrown at the same instant from the tops of two towers standing distance d apart. Ball A is thrown from the shorter tower, of height 10 m, at 10√2 m/s directed 45° above the horizontal toward the other tower. Ball B is thrown from the taller tower, of height 20 m, horizontally toward the first tower at 10 m/s. The two balls meet while both are still in the air. Find d.
items.figure_description: Two vertical towers stand on level ground, distance d apart. The left tower is 10 m tall; from its top, particle A is launched at 45° above the horizontal at 10√2 m/s, aimed toward the right tower. The right tower is 20 m tall; from its top, particle B is launched horizontally at 10 m/s, aimed toward the left tower.

solution.approach: Write the height of each particle above the ground as a function of time and find when the heights match; use that time to find the horizontal gap to close.

steps.text: Resolve particle A's launch velocity into horizontal and vertical parts.
Write the height of each particle above the ground as a function of time, measuring from its own tower.
Set the two heights equal and solve for the collision time; the −5t² term cancels on both sides.
At this time, A has moved a horizontal distance 10t toward B, and B has moved 10t toward A; together they cover the full gap d.

common_mistakes.text: Using only ball A's horizontal motion for the gap gives d = 10 m; adding ball B's 10 m motion toward A in the same time gives the correct d = 20 m.

items.question_text: Referring to the launch angles marked in the sketch, determine the projectile's time of flight and its range measured along the slope, with g = 10 m/s².
items.figure_description: A slope rises from left to right, meeting the horizontal ground at 30° (the angle is marked at the bottom-left corner, where the slope meets the ground). From a launch point partway up the slope a dashed horizontal reference line is drawn; the velocity arrow of 20√2 m/s starts at that point and points up and to the left, that is, away from the rising slope and toward the downhill side, making 45° with the dashed horizontal line.

solution.approach: Resolve the velocity and gravity along and perpendicular to the incline. Here the velocity points over the downhill side, so it makes 45°+30° with the incline surface.

steps.text: The launch point is on the incline, with a horizontal dashed line drawn through it. The velocity makes 45° with this horizontal line but points away from the slope on the downhill side, so the projectile lands lower down the incline.
steps.why_this_step: On the downhill side the incline surface itself runs below the horizontal, so the velocity angle from the slope adds the incline angle instead of subtracting it.

steps.text: Take axes along the incline, downhill taken as positive, and perpendicular to it, away from the surface taken as positive. Resolve the initial velocity and gravity into these two directions.
steps.equation: along incline: u cos75° ; perpendicular: u sin75° ; g along incline: g sin30° ; g perpendicular: g cos30°

steps.text: The projectile returns to the incline surface when the perpendicular displacement becomes zero again. This gives the time of flight.

Range along the incline is the along-incline distance covered in time T. Gravity's along-incline part adds to this motion here, since it also points down the slope. Time of flight and range along the incline are both stated below.

common_mistakes.text: Using the angle difference 45°−30° instead of the sum 45°+30° gives T ≈ 1.69 s and R ≈ 39.04 m, which is the answer for the projectile fired up the incline, not down it.
Ignoring the incline and using the flat-ground formulas T = 2u sinθ/g and R = u² sin2θ/g gives T = 4 s and R = 80 m, missing that the ground here is sloped.

items.question_text:
In the diagram, a projectile is launched from point O with speed 20√2 m/s directed 45° above the horizontal. The incline through O slopes downward at 37° to the horizontal, and the projectile comes down on this incline at point P.
(a) Determine how long the projectile is in the air before it lands on the sloped surface at P.
(b) Determine the distance OP, measured along the slope, from the launch point O to the landing point P.
items.figure_description: The particle leaves O with velocity 20√2 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. The slope through O runs downward at 37° to the horizontal, both close to O and at its lower end. The particle's curved path rises then falls, meeting the slope at point P, below and to the side of O. A right-angled construction with a vertical segment from O and a horizontal segment to P marks the drop and horizontal shift used to locate P.

solution.approach: Write the horizontal and vertical position as functions of time, then find where the path meets the incline's line through O, y = −x tan37°.

steps.text: Find the horizontal and vertical components of the launch velocity, taking the horizontal direction in which the incline descends as positive x.
Write the horizontal and vertical positions as functions of time, using g = 10 m/s².
The incline falls away below O at 37° in this direction, so P lies where the vertical position equals minus the horizontal position times tan37°.
Solve for the time of flight (part a).
Find x at this time, then divide by cos37° to get the distance along the incline. Restating both parts: the time of flight is 7 s and the range OP is 175 m.

common_mistakes.text: Using the equation for a particle landing above the launch point instead of below it, which gives t = 1 s and OP = 25 m.
